en: Will grieving for your only child bring good?
O warrior, can grief be repayment?
You gave your only child as a gift;
Can your promise become two?
Your falcon, your only light,
Has attained his desire.
This is God's decree:
Manas, your confidant and dear friend,
Has taken the falcon with him as a companion.”
So, grieving thus,
Kokboru went back to his people, they say.
With anguish lodged within him,
“My only child Koyonaaly has died,” he said.
To Khan Manas's funeral observances,
Kokboru did not come, they say.
“Because Kokboru has not come,”
Toshtuk did not come, they say.
Since Toshtuk did not come,
Khan Koshoi of the Katagan,
That khan did not come, they say.
Those who had made their promise firm,
All the khans—
And so, all of them failed
To come, they say!
Forty days had not yet passed since Khan Manas died,
Since the sovereign had departed—
The term of forty days was not yet full.
Then Abyke, his well-meaning kinsman,
Came to Bakai Khan:
“Uncle Bakai, leopard,
Let us not remain camped by the river;
With the khan dead, let us not all die,
Uncle Bakai, let us not be like an extinguished fire!
Uncle Bakai, I heard from those who came,
From the peoples of the three khans below:
Men have been killed; mares are being slaughtered;
I heard that a massacre has broken out.
Dear Uncle Bakai, let us go;
If someone has strayed somewhat,
Let us subdue him and set him straight.
They are the people mighty Manas left behind;
Let us go and keep them from destroying one another.
Slaughtering mares among them,
Slaughtering camels to make peace,
Speaking words of apology,
Saying, ‘Do not be enemies,’
Uncle Bakai, let us go
And bring in an impartial judge!”
Then Bakai said:
“My son Abyke, perish with your feast!
How can I go to his feast
And have them call Bakai accursed?
How can I go to your festivities?
May you perish with your gathering!
My son, how can I go to an assembly!
Bereft of his happiness,
‘There is that old smiling Bakai,’ they would say;
I would become a subject of gossip!
Yesterday my joy, Manas, told me:
‘With your white beard trailing,
Your eyes reddening like a raven's,
Do not go where you see a crowd,’ he said.
That is what my mountain-like one told me.
‘If people gather in an assembly,
My joy, dear Uncle Bakai,
Do not go near them,’ he said.
That is what my precious Manas told me:
‘My orphan's camels—
Herd them for him,’ he said.
I will not go to your gathering;
My joy, Manas, is no longer here;
I will not share in its ruin, my son!
Dear Abyke, I will not go to your assembly;
My mountain-like Manas, my hero, is gone;
Abyke, I will not enter your hell!
I will not turn away from Zhar-Konush;
When the khan died, to the old man
His camels became dear;
I will not part from the camels I tend!”
So saying then,
Bakai Khan sent Abyke on his way.
Ajybai of Argyn Khan—
Abyke, the kind-hearted kinsman,
Took him now as his companion
The three troubled khans—
He went to their quarrel.
Abyke had gone to mediate;
Let us leave him there
And turn to Semetey's grandfather, Khan Zhakyp;
Let us begin with that swinish khan.
Then in Khan Zhakyp's house
There was grain beer in a leather pail,
With burning poison mixed in.
In Khan Zhakyp's house
There was grain beer in a wooden tub,
With choking poison mixed in.
When your gray-maned Manas died,
Kobosh became sultan.
Those forty companions Manas left behind—
All forty were dogs from forty different places—
Had settled their encampment beside Kobosh.
Your Kobosh prayed to Bahauddin,
Vowed a sheep to Khorasan,
And, oh hero, grew swollen as a gray tick.
Over the Argyn and Kyrgyz peoples
Your Kobosh had become supreme sultan.
One day, what did poor Zhakyp do?
He fell into a rage
And summoned the honored Kobosh and Kochkor,
Gathering them all together.
With them came those old companions,
The forty companions of Khan Manas;
The accursed men came along too.
The six scoundrels and forty companions
Into Khan Zhakyp's palace
All gathered and entered.
“Come, my children, come,” he said,
“And heed the words I say.”
The strong spirits kept beside the wall,
A measure of spirits from a Kalmyk leather flask—
Zhakyp poured them without warning
And offered them to those six scoundrels and forty fools.
They became hopelessly drunk;
As the scoundrels stood there so,
Khan Zhakyp, with his wicked thoughts,
Said to the dogs:
“When a horse dies, you great dog,
Its rump hide is of use;
When an elder brother dies, his younger brother,
You great dog, has need of his sister-in-law.
I heard from those who came:
That insolent shrew Kanykey,
As a wife, divided their customs and disrupted the people;
As a girl, the shameless creature
Shook the world and disrupted the people.
Living widowed, she grew wild;
The shameless creature burned with lust
And ran utterly out of control.
I heard from those who came:
Six thousand silver ingots and a thousand beaver pelts
Bakai has taken as a bribe;
To Ormombek of Tekeche,
To a khan like Ormombek,
He will smuggle the bitch away, I heard.
The encampment by the river—
Could not one of you go and scout it?
Your inheritance left behind by Manas—
Consider that shrew:
You worthless men, could not one of you marry her?
Damn your fathers' graves, you six scoundrels!
Drink stones instead of spirits!
If that is not enough, you six scoundrels,
Mix in your father's blood and drink!”
Thus he was whetting their wickedness;
God had struck Zhakyp down.
“If she says she will marry, she is our sister-in-law;
Let us perform the marriage rite and take her.
If she says she will not marry, the shrew—
Let us drag her along the road
And have the dogs tear her apart.
Our father is like the Ala-Too;
Let us obey Khan Zhakyp
And go to that shameless woman.”
Unable to contain his excitement,
Kobosh blustered then,
Thundering in fury,
Making ready a coat no bullet could pierce,
Making ready a horse no bullet could reach.
Kyrgylchal was chief of the forty.
Shuutu the servant, his cap broad as a yurt felt,
Turned all the companions aside:
“Kyrgylchal, chief of the forty,
Consider it in your mind!
We companions came without horses;
For the companion who came without a horse,
Wild-sheep feet and copper forelegs—
He provided the finest horse to ride.
For the companion who came without a coat,
A golden collar and copper sleeves,
Double mail with rings like larks' eyes,
Striped cloth for battle, a roomy jacket—
He clothed him in the finest coat.
For the companion who came without a wife,
A thimble mouth, camel-calf eyes,
Great shining eyes that glanced about,
A crimson dress and a moon-slender waist—
A swaying beauty
Great Manas obtained for him.
For the companion who came without religion,
His voice when he cried out like the call to prayer,
His white turban as big as a cauldron—
Khan Manas provided a mullah.
Some of us companions came without a home.
For the companion who came without a home,
The upper edge of its lattice walls
Fastened with iron fittings,
All along the upper valance
Edged with beaver fur six fingerbreadths wide,
All its fastening bands
He had braided from pure silk;
He had a stately dwelling built to proper form—
Great Manas gave him a stately dwelling.
One companion came without livestock;
For the companion who came without livestock,
Horses with mottled heads on the foothills,
Thoroughbreds and swift steeds together,
Great Manas allotted them.
He joined what had been broken,
Gathered what had been scattered,
Kindled what had gone out,
Brought the dead to life.
Your hero Sultan Manas—
Clinging to his hem, we became men;
We became the equals of heroes' sons.
Dust rose wherever we went;
At our voices, souls departed.
Manas's salt carries a heavy debt;
Will his salt not destroy us?
Precious Manas's spirit—
Will his spirit not destroy us!
Kyrgylchal, chief of the forty,
Manas's salt is bitter;
How can we piss upon his salt?
Manas's spirit is golden;
How can we enter his camp?
As we speak, he has left behind
A noble male child;
How can we attack him?
Your khan, Manas the leopard—
While his spirit watches,
How can we attack his palace?!”
Then Kobosh blustered,
Thundering in fury:
“Always, you forty swine,
‘My lion Manas, blessed by Khydyr!’—
You shout that and leave it there!
Without even a moment's delay, forty companions,
Kyrgylchal and Tazbaimat,
You two must go at once
That wild shrew Kanykey—
Find out about the wretched woman!
If the bitch will not obey,
Drag her along the road
And have the dogs tear her apart!”
Having received his khan's command,
What could poor old Chalym do?
He slung a battle-axe at his waist
And took the familiar Tazbaimat
As his companion now.
To Khan Manas's palace
They rode and arrived.
Crying, “Oh, my gray-maned hero!”
Calling out mostly in mockery,
Whimpering, “Oh, my dear lost one!”
Swaying mostly in mockery.
Sixty women were singing laments;
